steps.message:
# Freeze store integrity maintenance

Ensure the `TextFileBasedViolationStore` maintains the integrity of its `stored.rules` index and files.

Setting `default.integrity` to `repair` will check the index and folder as they are on disk during initialization, even if the same folder was initialized before. Defaulting to `ignore` which checks nothing.

If an entry points to a path that is not a regular file directly within the folder, it is broken. This also applies if the file name is not a valid path.

If an entry is not broken and its file has no violations it is resolved. Files that only contain line breaks are also resolved.

Entries that point to the same file name are shared, even if nothing exists with that name. If multiple entries point to the same regular file they are also shared. Including through a symbolic or hard link. Even if that file is outside the folder.

The `TextFileBasedViolationStore` will not touch any shared entries or files that no entry points to. If an entry is shared and anything else it will remain shared.

When set to `repair` broken entries will be discarded without touching whatever they point to.

When set to `repair` resolved entries and the file they point to will be discarded. If a resolved entry is a symbolic link the file it points to will be deleted as well.

If using `repair` and saving no violations for a known rule it will forget the rule. Its entry will be removed and its file as well. Unless another entry is sharing that file. In which case only the entry will be removed. Even if it points outside the folder. If using `repair` and saving no violations for an unknown rule nothing will be saved.

If it cannot delete the file of a rule it is forgetting it will fail to save and leave the entry.

`FreezingArchRule` can help in these scenarios by recording all existing violations to a `ViolationStore`.
Consecutive runs will then only report new violations and ignore known violations.
If violations are fixed, `FreezingArchRule` will automatically reduce the known stored violations to prevent any regression.

==== Usage

To freeze an arbitrary `ArchRule` just wrap it into a `FreezingArchRule`:

[source,java,options="nowrap"]
----
ArchRule rule = FreezingArchRule.freeze(classes().should()./*complete ArchRule*/);
----

On the first run all violations of that rule will be stored as the current state. On consecutive runs only
new violations will be reported. By default `FreezingArchRule` will ignore line numbers, i.e. if a
violation is just shifted to a different line, it will still count as previously recorded
and will not be reported.

==== Configuration

By default `FreezingArchRule` will use a simple `ViolationStore` based on plain text files.
This is sufficient to add these files to any version control system to continuously track the progress.
You can configure the location of the violation store within `archunit.properties` (compare <<Advanced Configuration>>):

[source,options="nowrap"]
.archunit.properties
----
freeze.store.default.path=/some/path/in/a/vcs/repo
----

Furthermore, it is possible to configure

[source,options="nowrap"]
.archunit.properties
----
# must be set to true to allow the creation of a new violation store
# default is false
freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=true

# can be set to false to forbid updates of the violations stored for frozen rules
# default is true
freeze.store.default.allowStoreUpdate=false
----

This can help in CI environments to prevent misconfiguration:
For example, a CI build should probably never create a new the violation store, but operate on
an existing one.

As mentioned in <<Overriding configuration>>, these properties can be passed as system properties as needed.
For example to allow the creation of the violation store in a specific environment, it is possible to pass the system property via

[source,options="nowrap"]
----
-Darchunit.freeze.store.default.allowStoreCreation=true
----

It is also possible to allow all violations to be "refrozen", i.e. the store will just be updated
with the current state, and the reported result will be success. Thus, it is effectively the same behavior
as if all rules would never have been frozen.
This can e.g. make sense, because current violations are consciously accepted and should be added to the store,
or because the format of some violations has changed. The respective property to allow refreezing
all current violations is `freeze.refreeze=true`, where the default is `false`.

==== Extension

`FreezingArchRule` provides two extension points to adjust the behavior to custom needs.
The first one is the `ViolationStore`, i.e. the store violations will be recorded to. The second one
is the `ViolationLineMatcher`, i.e. how `FreezingArchRule` will associate lines of stored violations
with lines of actual violations. As mentioned, by default this is a line matcher that ignores the
line numbers of violations within the same class.

===== Violation Store

As mentioned in <<Configuration>>, the default `ViolationStore` is a simple text based store.
It can be exchanged though, for example to store violations in a database.
To provide your own implementation, implement `com.tngtech.archunit.library.freeze.ViolationStore` and
configure `FreezingArchRule` to use it. This can either be done programmatically:

[source,java,options="nowrap"]
----
FreezingArchRule.freeze(rule).persistIn(customViolationStore);
----

Alternatively it can be configured via `archunit.properties` (compare <<Advanced Configuration>>):

[source,options="nowrap"]
----
freeze.store=fully.qualified.name.of.MyCustomViolationStore
----

You can supply properties to initialize the store by using the namespace `freeze.store`.
For properties

[source,options="nowrap"]
----
freeze.store.propOne=valueOne
freeze.store.propTwo=valueTwo
----

arguments.new_string:
# can be set to false to forbid updates of the violations stored for frozen rules
# default is true
freeze.store.default.allowStoreUpdate=false

# can be set to repair to maintain the integrity of the violation store
# default is ignore
freeze.store.default.integrity=repair
----

This can help in CI environments to prevent misconfiguration:
For example, a CI build should probably never create a new the violation store, but operate on
an existing one.

With `freeze.store.default.integrity=repair` the store checks its index `stored.rules` and the
violation files on disk every time it is initialized:

* Entries pointing to anything other than a regular file directly within the store folder
  (e.g. missing files, directories or invalid file names) are broken and will be discarded,
  without touching whatever they point to.
* Entries whose file contains no violations (i.e. nothing but line breaks) are resolved and will be
  discarded together with their file (if the file is a symbolic link, together with the file it points to).
* Entries pointing to the same file name or the same regular file (also through symbolic or hard links)
  are shared and will never be touched, just like files that no entry points to.

Furthermore, a rule will be forgotten as soon as it has no violations left,
i.e. its entry will be removed together with its file (unless the file is shared with another entry).
Rules without any violations will then not be added to the store at all.

steps.message:
With `freeze.store.default.integrity=repair`, the `TextFileBasedViolationStore` now repairs `stored.rules` and the violation files as the spec describes. It defaults to `ignore`, which leaves behaviour unchanged. All 72 freeze tests pass, including 13 new ones. Nothing is committed yet.

**What `repair` does:**
- **On every `initialize`:** it re-reads `stored.rules` from disk, even if the same folder was set up earlier in the same JVM. It discards broken entries without touching what they point to. It discards resolved entries together with their file, including a symlink's target. It never touches shared entries or files that no entry points to.
- **On saving no violations:** for a known rule it removes the entry and its file, or only the entry if the file is shared. For an unknown rule it stores nothing. If the file can't be deleted, the save fails and the entry stays.

The code is in `TextFileBasedViolationStore.java`. I also documented the property in the class Javadoc and in `docs/userguide/008_The_Library_API.adoc`.

**Choices I made where the spec was silent:**
- **Unknown values:** anything other than `ignore` or `repair` (case-insensitive) fails initialization.
- **Store updates disabled:** with `allowStoreUpdate=false`, `repair` only logs a warning listing what it would fix, because that setting forbids changing any store file.
- **Entries pointing at `stored.rules`:** these count as shared, so they can never cause the index itself to be deleted.
- **Symlinked rule files:** the link is deleted first. If that fails, nothing changes. If the link goes but its target can't be deleted, the entry is still removed and a warning is logged.
- **Absolute paths:** all file lookups now go through one shared path helper. One side effect: an absolute path in a hand-edited `stored.rules` now means that absolute path; before, it was treated as a folder nested inside the store folder.
- **Saves are now serialized per store:** this stops a concurrent repair from discarding a new entry before its file is written.

**Behaviour to be aware of:** under `repair`, a rule that reaches zero violations is forgotten. If violations reappear later, `FreezingArchRule` sees a new rule and freezes them silently instead of reporting them. That follows from the spec, but it is a real change in meaning.

I couldn't run `spotlessCheck` because its formatter isn't cached for offline use. It only enforces unused-import removal, which I checked by hand.
